summary: Michigan's Lake Superior harbor-of-refuge front light: a bell tower moved from Point Iroquois, first lit 10 December 1895, and the 1919 Runnels rescue by keeper Otto Bufe.

light.characteristic: fixed white (1895); changed to fixed red in 1905; red flash every two seconds from 1922 (LighthouseFriends)

lens.where: sixth-order light lit 10 December 1895 (Board's list of lights); the front light's lens after 1895 is not described in the sources read

structures.note: Former bell tower from Point Iroquois, bolted to the west pier, capped with a decagonal iron lantern room; 43 ft tall (LighthouseFriends). Later replaced by a steel tower; date of replacement not given.

Rear range tower on the inner end of the west pier, nearly 62 ft tall, fifth-order Henry-Lepaute Fresnel (LighthouseFriends). Date conflicts: 18 July 1898 (LighthouseFriends) or 1899 (Board's 1899 report text).

access.note: LighthouseFriends visitor notes say the grounds are open and the towers closed. The Chamber of Commerce describes the stone pier as a fishing spot reached by a parking area by the low dunes. No source read gives a rule for the pier itself.

visit.note: LighthouseFriends visitor notes: grounds open, dwelling open in season, towers closed.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard operates and maintains the fog signal and rear range light on the pier (NPS brochure).

events.note: Former Point Iroquois bell tower set up at Grand Marais on the west pier
Fixed white light and fog bell placed in operation 10 December 1895 by Keeper Samuel F. Rogers
Act of 4 June 1897 allowed the Board to build a second (rear) light and complete the station for no more than $2,000 (LighthouseFriends)
Rear range light first exhibited 18 July 1898 (LighthouseFriends). The Board's annual report printed for 1899 gives 18 July 1899 (scan 220, printed p.169). The two sources disagree by a year.
Range lights changed from fixed white to fixed red; front tower moved seaward to the end of the extended pier (LighthouseFriends)
Storm of 6 January 1906 carried away roughly 250 ft of the new walkway; replaced the following May (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper's dwelling built; work began 10 June 1908 (LighthouseFriends)
Light station damaged in the 1913 storms; the group of stations' damage put at about $4,000 (Bulletin)

Steamer H. E. Runnels went ashore in a northwest gale on 14 November 1919; keeper Otto Buffe rendered assistance to the survivors; a Coast Guard surfman and volunteers assisted; no lives lost (Bulletin; NPS brochure)
Fog signal changed from a bell to an electric siren (Bulletin 1922; LighthouseFriends)
Front light changed from fixed red to a red flash every two seconds (LighthouseFriends)
Fog signal changed to an air diaphone, 12 June 1923 (LighthouseFriends)

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The NPS brochure and LighthouseFriends have Rogers keeping the light from December 1895. The USLHS roster starts him in 1898. LighthouseFriends's own roster also starts him in 1898, so its narrative and roster disagree.

The NPS brochure lists gold congressional medals for the head surfman, seven of his crew, one Coast Guardsman and four civilians. LighthouseFriends counts nine Coast Guardsmen and four local men. Both counts are reported; the story gives both.

LighthouseFriends gives 18 July 1898. The Board's annual report printed for 1899 (scan 220, printed p.169) reads 'July 18, 1899' on the page image. The two sources disagree by a year; no source read settles it.

The NPS brochure puts the rear range light on the pier and LighthouseFriends puts the rear tower on the inner end of the west pier; the Chamber of Commerce puts the rear light on shore behind the front light. Not resolved.

LighthouseFriends says the Historical Society received ownership of the 1908 keeper's dwelling in 1984, but its visitor notes give the dwelling's owner as the National Park Service. The NPS brochure says the Park Service owns the building that once served as the keepers quarters; the Chamber puts the museum in the keeper's house across the road. The sources agree the museum is in the keeper's house but not who owns it.

notes_for_editor: Checked 2026-10-22 against page images. LHB 1899 entry no. 298 is on scan leaf 220 (printed p.169), not 221 as the corpus index said; it reads 'exhibited on July 18, 1899'. LHB 1896-97 Point Iroquois entry 1399 is on scan 172 (printed 145), and the lights-established Grand Marais entry on scan 21 (printed 10); corpus scan numbers for this volume ran one leaf high. The 1893 (scan 210, printed 153), 1895 (scan 379, printed 156) and 1891-92 (scan 545, printed 170) citations were confirmed on the page image. The NRHP nomination for this station (reference 12000254) is a 'not yet digitized' placeholder in the cache, so it is not used. LighthouseFriends is the only source for the 1898 date and the 1897 act; the Board's 1899 entry conflicts with it. The USLHS roster begins Rogers in 1898 while LighthouseFriends and the NPS brochure say 1895. No newspaper search was run for Rogers. The Wikipedia article (inner and outer lights) was read for leads only and not cited. The LighthouseFriends account of Rogers's Navy service and an 1860 slave-trade capture is not used. The 1919 Bulletin spells the keeper 'Buffe'; the roster and LighthouseFriends say 'Bufe'; the story uses 'Bufe' and notes the variant. The 1913 Bulletin $4,000 figure is for the group of stations, not Grand Marais alone.
